welcome: Welcome to Zenith. Above you is the real sky, exactly as it is right now. Let's learn a few gestures, one at a time.
tut_palm: Open your left hand, and turn your palm toward your face. Your panel appears above it.
tut_fist: Now make a fist, to put the panel away.
tut_pick_h: Aim your right hand at a bright star, then pinch your thumb and finger to learn its name.
tut_pull: Pinch with both hands, and pull them apart. Time speeds up. Push them together to go back.
tut_pick_c: Aim the right controller at a bright star, and pull the trigger to learn its name.
tut_time: Push the right stick forward. The sky speeds up. Pull back to rewind.
tut_suit_h: Time to check your suit. Raise both open hands above your head, and look at the mirror.
tut_suit_c: Time to check your suit. Raise both controllers above your head, and look at the mirror.
tut_helmet_h: Touch the right side of your headset with your right hand to take your helmet off. Touch it again to put it back on.
tut_helmet_c: Touch the right side of your headset with the right controller to take your helmet off. Touch again to put it back on.
tut_launch_h: Ready for launch? Raise both fists above your head, and hold for a moment.
tut_launch_c: Ready for launch? Press Y on the left controller.
tut_higher_h: Want to go higher? Raise both fists above your head, and hold.
tut_higher_c: Want to go higher? Press Y on the left controller.
tut_end_h: You're ready. Push both palms down to come back to the ground. Open your left hand whenever you need the panel.
tut_end_c: You're ready. Press X to come back down. Your panel lives on the left controller.
suit_ok_h: Suit check complete. Looking good, astronaut.
suit_ok_c: Suit check complete. Looking good, astronaut.
place_iss: You are in orbit, four hundred and eight kilometres above Earth, moving at almost eight kilometres every second. Up here, you see a sunrise every hour and a half.
place_geo: You are thirty six thousand kilometres out, and the whole Earth fits in your view. At this height you keep pace with Earth's spin, so the same side always faces you.
selfie: Look at the drone, and smile.
b_Sun: The Sun, our star, about a hundred and fifty million kilometres away. Its light takes about eight minutes to reach you, so you always see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.
b_Moon: The Moon, about three hundred and eighty four thousand kilometres away. It always shows us the same face, because it turns exactly once for every trip around Earth.
b_Mercury: Mercury, the smallest planet, and the closest to the Sun. A year there lasts just eighty eight Earth days.
b_Venus: Venus, the brightest planet in our sky. Its thick clouds trap heat, making it the hottest planet of all, even hotter than Mercury.
b_Mars: Mars, the red planet. Its colour comes from rust in its dust. It also has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons.
b_Jupiter: Jupiter, the largest planet. More than a thousand Earths would fit inside it, and its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than our whole planet.
b_Saturn: Saturn, famous for its rings of ice and rock. It is so light for its size, it would float in a big enough bathtub.
b_Uranus: Uranus, an ice giant tipped on its side, so it rolls around the Sun like a ball.
b_Neptune: Neptune, the farthest planet. Its winds are the fastest in the solar system, faster than the speed of sound on Earth.
s_11767: Polaris, the North Star. It sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so while the whole sky turns, Polaris barely moves. Travellers have used it to find north for centuries.
s_32349: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It is less than nine light years away, one of our closest neighbours.
s_27989: Betelgeuse, the red supergiant on Orion's shoulder. If it took the Sun's place, it would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
s_91262: Vega, a bright blue-white star. In about thirteen thousand years, Earth's slow wobble will make Vega our North Star.
s_24436: Rigel, the blue-white foot of Orion. It shines tens of thousands of times brighter than our Sun.
s_80763: Antares, the red heart of the Scorpion. Its name means rival of Mars, because the two look so alike.
s_69673: Arcturus, an orange giant, and the brightest star in the northern half of the sky.
s_21421: Aldebaran, the glowing orange eye of Taurus, the bull.
s_30438: Canopus, the second brightest star in the night sky. Spacecraft have used it as a guide star to keep their bearings.
s_97649: Altair, the eagle's star. With Vega and Deneb, it forms the Summer Triangle.
s_102098: Deneb, the tail of the swan. It looks faint next to Vega, but it is truly one of the most powerful stars you can see, thousands of light years away.
c_Ori: Orion, the hunter. Look for the three stars in a row, his belt. Just below hangs his sword, where the Orion Nebula is making new stars right now.
c_UMa: Ursa Major, the great bear. Seven of its stars form the Big Dipper, known in India as the Saptarishi, the seven sages.
c_Sco: Scorpius, the scorpion, with red Antares at its heart and a long curling tail.
c_Cru: Crux, the Southern Cross, the smallest constellation of all. Its long arm points toward the south pole of the sky.
c_Cas: Cassiopeia, the queen. Her five bright stars make a W, opposite the Big Dipper across the North Star.
